name: generalization
quote: I've observed that birds have feathers.
description: Ability to perceive a common attribute from a set of experiences or ideas.
results: notice a similarity, establish a pattern to be used in the future
examples: Every time I'm around that cat, I sneeze.

variations.name: stereotyping
variations.description: Predicting that every member of a groups share all characteristics perceived to be common within the group.
perceptions: This person, place, or thing is similar in some ways to something I've experienced before.
results: assume that the person, place, or thing shares other characteristics

guidance.description: Stereotypes can be accurate statements about current statistical group differences, but they can be inaccurate when applied to individuals.

variations.name: analogizing
variations.description: Understanding a pattern in one thing by making reference to a pattern from something else.
perceptions: An aspect of this thing seems similar to an aspect of something else.
Drawing attention to that partial similarity helps me better understand.

guidance.description: The use of analogies and metaphors can help people understand new or complex topics.

commentaries.quote: 'Generalization' as used here is just the thing that neurons do in the brain - they create patterns of connections that reflect some aspect of the world.  This might be similar in concept to 'inductive reasoning', but there's no feedback loop -- even a fish can link patterns together: repeat things that worked well, avoid things that hurt.
Just linking perceptions to results often leads to errors. A rain dance does not always bring rain. Stereotypes are what the brain does, but it can be helpful to re-evaluate established patterns.
Analogies and metaphors are the underdogs of science communication, making the complex comprehensible and the tricky tangible.
One good analogy is worth three hours discussion.
Metaphors provide the illusion of knowledge, so they must be used with care.
